title: Spring Lecture #2: Build Your First Spring Boot Application

questions.question: In the address `192.168.1.10:8080`, what does `8080` identify?
options: The machine on the network that should receive the data
The application on that machine that should receive the data
The HTTP method the browser will use
The version of the HTTP protocol in use
questions.explanation: The IP address brings data to the correct machine; the port number lets the operating system hand it to the right application on that machine (e.g. a Spring Boot app listening on 8080). Identifying the machine is the IP address's job, not the port's.

questions.question: On Spring Initializr you see a Spring Boot version ending in `-SNAPSHOT`. What does that mean?
options: It is the latest fully tested stable release recommended for production
It is a release candidate that only needs final documentation
It is a long-term-support release with extended security fixes
It is a work-in-progress build that may contain bugs and is not final
questions.explanation: A SNAPSHOT is a work-in-progress version and is not considered final. RC (Release Candidate) is almost ready but still not the final release. For learning and real projects the notes recommend choosing a stable release.

questions.question: A user types `https://www.coderarmy.in` into the browser without any port number. Which port does the browser connect to?
options: Whatever port DNS returns with the IP address
questions.explanation: When no port is written, the browser uses the protocol's default: 443 for HTTPS and 80 for HTTP. DNS only resolves the domain name to an IP address; it does not supply the port. 8080 is just Spring Boot's default for local development, which is why we type it explicitly.

questions.question:
Given the lecture project's `application.properties` and controller below, which URL returns `

Hello World

`?
options: http://localhost:8080/hello
http://localhost:9090/demo/hello
http://localhost:9090/hello
http://localhost:9090/HelloController/hello
questions.explanation: `server.port=9090` makes the embedded Tomcat listen on 9090 instead of the default 8080, and `@GetMapping("hello")` maps GET `/hello`. `spring.application.name` only names the application; it does not add a `/demo` prefix to URLs. The class name is not part of the path either.

questions.question: Why can a Spring Boot web application packaged as a JAR be started directly (e.g. with `java -jar`) instead of being deployed into a separately installed server?
options: Because the JVM itself understands HTTP once a class is annotated with `@RestController`
Because the JAR contains the application together with the setup it needs, including an embedded server
Because JAR packaging converts the application into a native operating-system executable
Because Spring Initializr installs Tomcat globally on the machine when the project is generated
questions.explanation: A Spring Boot JAR bundles your code with what is required to run it, and with the web dependency that includes an embedded Tomcat that Spring Boot starts for you. That is why you never installed Tomcat yet saw "Tomcat started on port 8080". The JVM alone still does not understand HTTP, and Initializr only generates a project skeleton.

questions.question: In the flow of a request to `localhost:8080/hello`, which component matches the path `/hello` to the `sayHello()` method?
options: The browser, which looks up the method name in the URL
The operating system, using the port number
The embedded Tomcat server, which reads `application.properties`
Spring MVC, which checks the registered request mappings
questions.explanation: The notes split the work: Spring Boot starts and configures the application, embedded Tomcat listens on the port and receives the HTTP request, and Spring MVC checks its mappings and calls the matching controller method. The OS only uses the port to deliver data to the right application; Tomcat does not know about your `@GetMapping` methods by itself.

questions.question: You start the lecture app while another copy of it is still running, and startup fails saying port 9090 is already in use. What is the correct fix?
options: Stop the other instance, or give this one a different `server.port` in `application.properties`
Rename `spring.application.name` so the two apps no longer conflict
Change `@GetMapping("hello")` to a different path so the endpoints do not clash
Run the app from `localhost` instead of `127.0.0.1`, because they use separate ports
questions.explanation: A port identifies one listening application on a machine, so two servers cannot both listen on 9090. Either free the port or configure another one with `server.port`. The application name and endpoint paths have nothing to do with the port, and `localhost` is just another name for `127.0.0.1`, the same machine.

questions.question: With the lecture's controller below, the app is running on port 9090. What happens when you open `http://localhost:9090/bye` in a browser?
options: Error 404, because the method is named `greetBye`, so the URL must be `/greetBye`

Error, because Spring looks for an HTML template file named `

Bye

` to render
`greetBye()` runs and the returned string is written directly into the response body, so the page shows "Bye" as a heading

The browser downloads a JSON object `{"greetBye": "

Bye

"}`
questions.explanation:
The URL comes from the `@GetMapping` value, not the method name, so `/bye` maps to `greetBye()`. In a `@RestController` every method's return value is written straight to the response body (it behaves as `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody`), so the browser receives the text `

Bye

` and renders it as a heading. Looking up a template by the returned name is what a plain `@Controller` does, not `@RestController`.

questions.question: The log says `Tomcat started on port 9090`. Request A to `http://localhost:8080/hello` shows "This site can't be reached"; request B to `http://localhost:9090/hellooo` returns 404 Not Found. What do these two symptoms tell you?
options: Both mean the controller was not detected by Spring
A never reached any application because nothing listens on 8080; B reached Tomcat, but Spring MVC found no mapping for that path
A means the URL path is wrong, and B means the application is not running
Both mean the embedded Tomcat failed to start
questions.explanation: "Can't be reached" means no application accepted the connection on that port - a wrong-port problem, since the app is on 9090. A 404 is an HTTP response, so the request did reach the running server; it just found no mapping for `/hellooo`. Telling these layers apart is exactly why the notes say internals matter for debugging.

questions.question: In the lecture's `DemoApplication`, the commented-out lines are enabled. What happens when the application is started?
options: Compilation fails, because a class annotated with `@RestController` cannot be created with `new`
Nothing is printed, because `hello()` only executes when an HTTP request arrives
Startup fails, because Spring already created a `HelloController` and a second instance is not allowed

After startup, `

Hello World

` is printed to the console, and the server keeps serving requests
questions.explanation: `SpringApplication.run` starts the context and the embedded Tomcat, then returns; the next lines are ordinary Java, so `hello()` is called like any method and its string is printed. Annotations do not stop you from using `new`, and creating your own object does not conflict with the one Spring manages. The server stays up because Tomcat keeps running after `main` continues.
